paras: The Pelham gambling-house raid shooting took place on August 1, 1910, when a sheriff's posse and Pelham officers fired into a house near Pelham, Georgia, where a group of Black men were said to be gambling. Between one and three of the men were reported killed and several more wounded, and no white man was hurt. Two wire versions with different death tolls ran in papers from Alabama to New York, and a Georgia follow-up described fears of a 'general riot' in the town.

On the afternoon or evening of Monday, August 1, officers at Pelham were told that a crowd of Black men was gambling or 'causing a disturbance' at a house on the edge of town. The Savannah special placed the house about two miles from Pelham, while one reprint said five miles.

According to the Savannah special, Sheriff Shockley summoned a posse and found the men, who had learned of its coming, barricaded in the house. The posse surrounded the house and the sheriff ordered the men to surrender; the dispatch said they answered by firing, and the posse returned fire, 'completely riddling the house with bullets.' After the men asked for quarter, the posse entered and, by this account, found two dead, three almost dying and four unharmed under the beds.

A second dispatch told of half a dozen officers raiding a house where about a dozen men were reported gambling, and said the men opened fire when the officers appeared. In this version the officers' return fire killed James Brooks, fatally wounded Charles Boyd and wounded two others; five men were captured and one wounded man escaped. Both versions came from the officers' side, and none reported any white man hurt.

A Pelham dispatch of August 4 in the Brunswick News said the 'racial feeling' stirred by the shooting had subsided and the danger of a further outbreak was past, although a general riot had at first been feared. It reported that one of the wounded, James Brown, had died and that Charles Boyd was in critical condition, while the others were expected to recover. This account credited the raid to the deputy sheriff and Pelham policemen with several special deputies, sent to arrest a 'gang of crap shooters'. No report of an inquest, charges against the officers, or prosecution of the captured men was found.

The story reached white papers on August 2 by two routes, and both took the officers' account as fact. The Savannah special, printed in New York and Washington and reprinted in Prescott and in Mathews, Virginia, called the men 'disorderly negroes' and ran under headlines such as 'POSSE STORMS FORT, SHOOTING NEGROES' and 'NEGROES DEFY POSSE'. The other dispatch, carried in Montgomery, Birmingham, Pensacola, Washington and Newark, framed it as a 'RAID' and named the dead and dying men.

Most papers gave the episode one or two sentences, sometimes appended to other stories of armed clashes between officers and Black men, as the East St. Louis Daily Journal did with an Ohio police battle. Only the Brunswick News, in Georgia, followed up, and it headlined the episode as a 'RACIAL CLASH' that had quieted. No coverage of the shooting was found in the Black press.

The death toll was never settled in the coverage: the Savannah special said two were killed and three probably fatally wounded, the other wire said one was killed and one was dying, and the August 4 dispatch spoke of 'three negroes' killed while its subhead said one was dead. The Brunswick News named the man who died of his wounds as James Brown, while the first-day dispatch named the dead man James Brooks, possibly the same person.

reader.title: Pelham gambling-house raid shooting
bases: Every version describes a sheriff's posse, police, or deputy sheriff with special deputies shooting into a house of Black men they had come to arrest for gambling or a disturbance, killing one to three (A1, A2, A13).

Two independently worded wire versions and a later Georgia dispatch agree that officers and a posse raided a house near Pelham on Aug. 1 and shot several Black men, though they differ on numbers (A1, A2, A13).

accounts.label: Savannah special from Pelham (sheriff's side)
accounts.gist: Sheriff Shockley heard of a disturbance, summoned a posse, found the men barricaded, ordered them to surrender, was fired on, and riddled the house until they asked for quarter; two were dead, three dying, four unharmed under beds.

accounts.label: Pelham wire (officers' raid)
accounts.gist: Half a dozen officers raided a house where a dozen men were reported gambling; the men opened fire, and the officers' return fire killed James Brooks, fatally wounded Charles Boyd and wounded two others; five were captured and one wounded man escaped.

accounts.label: Pelham dispatch of Aug. 4
accounts.gist: The deputy sheriff, policemen and special deputies went to arrest crap shooters in an outhouse and were answered with gunfire; racial feeling ran high and a riot was feared, but the town had quieted; James Brown had since died and Charles Boyd was critical.

framing.detail: The Savannah special called the men 'disorderly negroes' and 'Disturbers' and ran under 'POSSE STORMS FORT, SHOOTING NEGROES', presenting the posse's version without question.
Most papers ran one or two sentences from either wire under headlines like 'TWO NEGROES KILLED' or 'FOUR NEGROES SHOT, ONE DEAD, IN GEORGIA RAID.'
The Brunswick News headlined 'PELHAM AGAIN QUIET AFTER RACIAL CLASH', treating the shooting as a racial disturbance that had subsided.

versions.value: 'three' killed and two fatally wounded; one wounded man later died

conflicts.note: The Aug. 4 Georgia dispatch is latest and local but internally inconsistent: its subhead says one dead, its lead three; it reports one wounded man (James Brown) died after the first reports.

versions.value: deputy sheriff, policemen and special deputies

conflicts.note: The versions can be reconciled as officers leading deputized citizens; only the Savannah special names the sheriff.
The five-mile figure appears only in one reprint of the special.
Possibly the same man with a variant surname; the coverage does not settle it.
